relations.myth: Satī manifests ten forms around Śiva
relations.note: Satī projects the Mahāvidyās as her forms or companions.

relations.myth: Satī surrounds Śiva with ten forms
relations.note: The Mahāvidyās block Śiva’s escape until he yields to Satī.

relations.myth: Dakṣa excludes Satī and Śiva from sacrifice
relations.note: Dakṣa’s exclusion precipitates Satī’s manifestation of the Mahāvidyās.

relations.myth: Pārvatī blocks ten exits with her forms
relations.note: A modern oral account makes the Mahāvidyās forms projected by Pārvatī.

relations.myth: Kālī fills every direction as Śiva leaves
relations.note: A modern retelling derives the other Mahāvidyās as directional forms of Kālī.
After Śiva submits, Tārā merges into Kālī while the other forms disappear.
Modern harmonization presents the Mahāvidyās as battle forms produced by Durgā.

relations.myth: Śākambharī emits battle powers against Durgama
relations.note: The Mahāvidyās issue from Śatākṣī-Śākambharī among numerous goddess powers.
The emitted Mahāvidyās join Śākambharī’s forces against Durgama.
Brahmā uses the Mahāvidyās’ powers like an arm to create.
Viṣṇu uses the Mahāvidyās’ powers like an arm to preserve.
At Kāmarūpa, Kālī-Kāmākhyā’s lotus throne is identified as Brahmā.
At Kāmarūpa, Kālī-Kāmākhyā’s lion throne is identified as Viṣṇu.
At Kāmarūpa, Kālī-Kāmākhyā sits upon a corpse identified as Śiva.

relations.myth: Kālī stands upon or unites with Śiva
relations.note: Kālī stands on, sexually unites with, or is paired with Śiva-Mahākāla.
At Tārāpīṭh, Tārā nurses Śiva after poison afflicts him.
The text assigns Akṣobhya as Tārā’s male partner.

relations.myth: Buddha-Viṣṇu teaches Tārā worship at Mahācīna
relations.note: A Buddha-form of Viṣṇu teaches the transgressive rites of Tārā.

relations.myth: Vasiṣṭha seeks Tārā rites at Mahācīna
relations.note: Vasiṣṭha curses Tārā, then travels to learn her left-hand worship.
Tripurasundarī is paired with Śiva in his Kāmeśvara form.
The five Brahmans form the supports and surface of Tripurasundarī’s couch.
The text assigns three-eyed Śiva-Tryambaka as Bhuvaneśvarī’s partner.
The text assigns five-faced Dakṣiṇāmūrti as Bhairavī’s partner.
Tantric sources treat Bhairava as Bhairavī’s male counterpart.

relations.myth: Chinnamastā stands upon copulating Kāma and Rati
relations.note: Chinnamastā stands or dances upon Kāma during reversed intercourse with Rati.

relations.myth: Chinnamastā stands upon copulating Kāma and Rati
relations.note: Chinnamastā stands or dances upon Rati during reversed intercourse with Kāma.

relations.myth: Chinnamastā feeds attendants with her blood
relations.note: One lateral blood stream from Chinnamastā’s neck feeds Ḍākinī.

relations.myth: Chinnamastā feeds attendants with her blood
relations.note: One lateral blood stream from Chinnamastā’s neck feeds Varṇinī.

relations.myth: Headless Kabandha Śiva worshipped beside Chinnamastā
relations.note: The text prescribes worship of headless Kabandha Śiva beside Chinnamastā.
Chinnamastā and Buddhist Chinnamuṇḍā share self-decapitation, three blood streams, and two attendants.
Buddhist traditions associate Chinnamuṇḍā’s self-decapitation imagery with the adept Mekhalā.
Buddhist traditions associate Chinnamuṇḍā’s self-decapitation imagery with the adept Kanakhalā.
One version identifies Dhūmāvatī as Pārvatī’s smoky widowed form.
Dhūmāvatī arises when Pārvatī swallows Śiva and smoke issues from her.
After emerging, Śiva requires the husband-consuming goddess to bear widowhood’s marks.

relations.myth: Tripurasundarī emanates Bagalāmukhī from turmeric lake
relations.note: Tripurasundarī emits Bagalāmukhī in response to Viṣṇu’s austerities.
Viṣṇu performs austerities, prompting Bagalāmukhī’s emanation to halt the storm.
Bagalāmukhī neutralizes the demon’s speech-siddhi by grasping his tongue.
Before Bagalāmukhī kills him, Madana gains depiction or worship beside her.
In some versions, substances associated with disguised Śiva help generate Mātaṅgī.
In some versions, leftovers or substances associated with Pārvatī generate Mātaṅgī.
Mātaṅgī is identified or paralleled with Sarasvatī as transgressive divine speech.
Kamalā, as Lakṣmī, is Viṣṇu’s consort, though Mahāvidyā images usually omit him.
The text assigns a Viṣṇu-form of Sadāśiva as Kamalā’s partner.
Variable lists align the ten Mahāvidyās pairwise with Viṣṇu’s ten avatāras.
